faqs.a: SVG optimization (minification) removes everything the browser does not need to render the graphic: XML comments, whitespace between tags, and redundant spacing. The shapes stay exactly the same.
faqs.q: What does optimizing an SVG mean?

faqs.a: Comments, indentation and line breaks are invisible to the renderer but still download with the file. On icon-heavy sites, trimming them across dozens of files adds up to real bandwidth savings.
faqs.q: Why do comments and whitespace matter?

faqs.a: No. The optimizer only removes comments and collapses whitespace. It does not touch path data, colors or coordinates, so the rendered result is pixel-identical.
faqs.q: Will optimization change how my SVG looks?

faqs.a: The drawing is unchanged, so you can safely replace the original. Keep a readable copy in your source files if you edit SVGs by hand often.
faqs.q: Should I keep the original file?

faqs.a: Very large SVGs with thousands of paths may need a more aggressive optimizer that also simplifies path data. This tool covers the safe, common 10–40% savings.
faqs.q: What if my file is huge?

faqs.a: No. Parsing and minifying happen entirely in your browser tab.

svg-optimizer.formula:
saved bytes = original bytes − optimized bytes
saved % = saved bytes ÷ original bytes × 100

Typical result: 10–40% smaller, depending on comments and formatting.

svg-optimizer.workedExample:
You paste an SVG that is 2,480 bytes with comments and heavy indentation.

The optimizer removes a 96-byte comment, collapses 320 bytes of inter-tag whitespace and trims 30 bytes of redundant spacing.

Optimized size = 2,480 − (96 + 320 + 30) = 2,034 bytes.
Saved = 446 bytes; saved % = 446 ÷ 2,480 × 100 = 18.0%.

The side-by-side previews look identical, and the downloaded file is 446 bytes lighter on every page load.
